body_markdown:
## A Hypothetical Scenario


Consider a hypothetical: a shift supervisor at a 60-person specialty metal fabrication shop is let go after the company consolidates two production lines into one. It is not a for-cause termination. The employer offers a modest severance payment tied to years of service, and the employee is owed 47 hours of accrued, unused PTO under company policy. All three pay elements, the last regular wages for hours already worked, the PTO payout, and the severance, are scheduled to go out on the same final check.


For the payroll administrator running that check, this is not a routine pay cycle. It is three different kinds of pay converging on one employee record, under a compressed deadline, with FICA withholding that has to be right on all three.


## When a Routine Pay Cycle Becomes a Termination Event


Most payroll teams have per-paycheck FICA calculation down to a science. Social Security and Medicare withholding on regular wages, matched by the employer, deposited on schedule, happens every pay period without much drama. Termination changes the shape of the problem. The pay event is no longer "the usual amount, on the usual date." It includes wage types that do not show up in a normal cycle, on a timeline that is often faster than a normal cycle, for an employee who will not be on the next payroll run to catch a correction.


That combination, unusual wage types plus a compressed deadline plus no next-cycle safety net, is what makes this moment worth handling deliberately rather than treating it as a slightly bigger version of a regular paycheck.


## Severance Pay Is FICA Taxable Wages


It is a common assumption that severance is somehow outside the normal payroll tax system, treated more like a settlement or a gift than a paycheck. It is not. Severance pay is wages for FICA purposes, meaning it is subject to Social Security and Medicare withholding on the employee side and to the employer's matching contribution, the same as regular wages. The U.S. Supreme Court settled this question directly in[United States v. Quality Stores, Inc.](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/572/141/) , 572 U.S. 141 (2014), ruling unanimously that severance pay is FICA-taxable wages rather than a category exempt from payroll tax. It gets folded into the employee's FICA taxable wages for the year rather than carved out as something separate.


That single point trips up more final-pay calculations than almost anything else in this process. A departing employee, or even a well-meaning manager negotiating an exit package, may expect severance to arrive at a clean, round number. Payroll has to explain, and calculate, that severance is taxable wages rather than a tax-free parting gift, before that number gets finalized.


## The Final Paycheck Often Cannot Wait


The second complication is timing. Many employers are used to running payroll on a fixed, predictable schedule, biweekly, semimonthly, whatever the standard cycle is. A termination frequently breaks that schedule. Depending on the state and the circumstances of the separation, a final paycheck may need to be issued well ahead of the next regularly scheduled payroll run, sometimes within days, sometimes immediately.


Final-pay timing rules vary meaningfully from state to state, and by whether the separation was voluntary or involuntary, so there is no single deadline that applies everywhere. As the[U.S. Department of Labor's final paycheck guidance](https://www.dol.gov/general/topic/wages/lastpaycheck) confirms, there is no federal law setting one deadline for the last paycheck; timing is a matter of state law, which is exactly why the rule that applies to one departure will not necessarily apply to the next. The point for a payroll or HR leader is not to memorize one rule and assume it travels. It is to recognize that "when does this check need to go out" is a separate question from "how is the check calculated," and both questions have to be answered correctly, often on short notice, for every departure.


## Three Kinds of Pay, One FICA Calculation


Put those two pieces together and the fabrication shop scenario comes into focus. The final check has to combine regular wages for hours worked, an accrued PTO payout, and a severance payment, and all three are FICA taxable wages that need to be captured, withheld, and matched correctly, on a timeline that may not match the company's normal pay cycle.


If any one of those three pay types gets treated as a manual side calculation, built in a spreadsheet outside the regular payroll system because "it's just this one employee, this one time," the risk of an error goes up. A missed or understated FICA withholding on a final check does not just create an employee-facing problem. It creates an employer-side reporting and remittance problem that has to be reconciled later, often after the employee is long gone and unavailable to help sort it out.


## Why This Moment Trips Up Payroll and HR Teams


This is exactly the kind of exception payroll leaders describe when they talk about what keeps them up at night, avoiding missed filings and penalties and staying ahead of missed deadlines and agency notices, especially when a pay event falls outside the normal weekly or biweekly rhythm. HR leaders carry a parallel version of the same worry, falling behind on a compliance step during an already-emotional employee exit, or having a manager handle an off-cycle detail inconsistently because nobody flagged that this termination needed different handling than a routine one.


Terminations are also, by nature, unscheduled compared to a normal payroll run. That is precisely why they are handled under time pressure, with less margin to double-check the math than a routine cycle offers.


## Keeping the Termination Record and the Pay Run Connected


Back to the fabrication shop. The reason this scenario resolves cleanly rather than becoming a reconciliation headache three months later comes down to whether the termination and the final pay run are treated as one connected event or two separate ones.


In AsureCentral, a termination event and the final pay run stay on the same employee record, so severance, final wages, and the PTO payout calculate together instead of being assembled as a manual, off-system calculation under deadline pressure. The payroll administrator is not exporting a spreadsheet, applying a separate FICA calculation to the severance amount, and hoping it lines up with what the system already knows about the employee's regular wages and PTO balance. It is one record, one calculation, one final check.


## When the Timeline Is Too Tight to Handle Alone


Not every company has a payroll team with the bandwidth to build a correct off-cycle final pay run on 48 hours' notice, especially a leaner team that is also managing the rest of a normal pay cycle at the same time. For an employer in that position, AsureWorks gives a way to have Asure specialists run that off-cycle final pay event, including the FICA treatment of severance and PTO payout, rather than assembling it in-house under time pressure. It is a managed service, not a co-employment arrangement. The employer stays the employer of record and keeps control over the severance decision itself. Asure handles the mechanics of getting the pay event calculated and processed correctly.


## Where This Fits in the Bigger Picture


Routine, per-paycheck FICA calculation, the kind that runs on autopilot every pay period, is its own subject, and Asure has already covered it in depth as one of five procedures in a broader guide on managing payroll deductions as a company grows. That guide's second procedure, FICA Calculation and Remittance, covers how employee Social Security and Medicare withholdings and employer matching contributions get computed each pay cycle and deposited through EFTPS. This piece has deliberately stayed off that ground. The termination moment, severance treated as FICA taxable wages, an accelerated final-pay timeline, and PTO payout landing in the same check, is a narrower, less-routine problem that deserves its own attention.

## Getting the Last Paycheck Right


An employee's last paycheck is not the moment to improvise. It is a FICA taxable pay event with its own timing pressure, built from wage types a normal cycle rarely combines, for an employee who will not be there to catch a mistake on the next run.


For payroll and HR leaders who want the termination record and the final pay run to stay on the same system rather than becoming a manual side project, AsureCentral keeps that calculation connected. For teams who would rather hand the off-cycle final pay event to specialists during an already-urgent departure, AsureWorks is built for exactly that scenario, without asking the employer to give up employer-of-record status to get the help.


## Related Questions


**Is severance subject to FICA?**


Yes. Severance pay is FICA-taxable wages, not a tax-free settlement or gift. In[United States v. Quality Stores, Inc.](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/572/141/) , 572 U.S. 141 (2014), the U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously that severance pay is subject to Social Security and Medicare withholding on the employee side and the employer's matching contribution, the same as regular wages. That holding applies regardless of how the severance amount is calculated or framed in an exit package.
